items.content_html:

items.title: Apple's 'Harbor' app will make running local AI across multiple Macs trivial
items.content_html:
An app presently called "Harbor" will help turn multiple Macs into a private AI inference server, keeping data local while also making the process of creating an AI server much easier.

The Mac has become a very useful tool for AI research, but it could be even more useful. Apple is working on an app that can make it easier to run large language models (LLMs) locally, so long as you have enough processing power and memory available.

Formerly known as Fabric, Harbor is the app that creates a private AI inference server on a Mac, according to Aaronp613 on X. It is capable of running open-weight models on the Mac itself, and apparently is extremely user-friendly.

Apple is working on a new app called Harbor

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon— your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.

Set up in minutes, not hours Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you're running— no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.

Download and run models directly Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.

Cluster for scale Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer's capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.

Harbor is currently in a private preview under the Claris brand.

— Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026

The installation requires just a few minutes to complete, with seemingly no need to manually configure anything or use a command line. Harbor manages the model on behalf of the user, including handling the downloads directly.

If there is more than one Mac available, they can be connected as a cluster over Thunderbolt 5. These are automatically detected by Harbor, which deals with the inter-device connection and the now larger pool of unified memory.

End users shouldn't expect to see the app anytime soon. Harbor is currently in "private preview" under Apple's Claris brand.

A massive help for AI development

Like pretty much any new technology trend, it can be difficult to get into working with AI. Especially if you don't want to deal with cloud-based services.

Not everyone wants to simply hand their data over to OpenAI or Anthropic in exchange for their services. Making a local LLM server eliminates that, but at a fairly high financial cost of new hardware.

But at the same time, there's also the work that needs to be put in to get the server up and running. If you have multiple Macs available, clustering them together to handle tougher workloads is a possibility.

Apple has already provided some software assistance, with MLX using Thunderbolt networking to cluster devices together for this purpose. Later, Apple made changes to macOS and MLX to include Thunderbolt 5 support as well as the introduction of GPU-based neural accelerator support.

In October 2026, it also detailed a new Minions system that uses idle GPUs in Apple Silicon Macs and turning them into a dynamic virtual GPU cloud.

Harbor appears to be an attempt focused on making the process of getting things going, rather than improving the performance of AI. While it may not make queries run faster, it's a change that should make the entire system much easier to get going in the first place.

items.title: Football Manager 27 Touch leads Apple Arcade's winter updates
items.content_html:
Apple Arcade subscribers get a new "Football Manager "game to play today, with four more titles on the way on December 3.

Gamers who pay for Apple Arcade are getting a big name in sports added to the service on November 11. "Football Manager 27 Touch" is a continuation of the managerial soccer series, with the game made for iPhone and iPad gameplay.

For the 27 iteration, there's a new Match Engine that gives more ways to change what happens during games. New Recruitment and Match Preparation tools will help with scouting and planning the matches themselves.

There's also a new iPhone interface, redesigned so most of the controls are within reach of your thumb.

December updates

While "Football Manager 27 Touch" is playable now, Apple has also got a bunch of games being prepared for launch on December 3, in time for the holidays.

The list includes "Plants vs Zombies: Replanted," which reworks the classic game with new levels and modes. There's also local co-op and PVP handled on the same device, with the exclusive Party Mode also giving the yard a makeover.

"solitaire(ish)" comes from Playstack, the publishers of "Balatro," and follows similar roguelike deck-building lines as the blockbuster hit. Players must build stacks to reach gradually rising score goals, while at the same time upgrading their decks using more than 150 special cards.


Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown+

"Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown+" is Ubisoft's revival of its platformer. For Apple Arcade, the version includes all the released downloadable content, including the Mask of Darkness story expansion.

Lastly, "Lego Duplo Playtime" is a brick-building game intended for younger users. Using Lego Duplo bricks, players can construct their own buildings and worlds, and even custom characters.

Apple Arcade is available for $6.99 per month, with a one-month free trial. It is also included under Apple One plans, including the $21.95 Individual plan, $27.95 Family, and $39.95 Premier options.

items.title: Adobe MAX brings new editing tools and more AI to Creative Cloud
items.content_html:
From relighting photos to separating overlapping dialogue, Adobe's latest tools give Photoshop, Premiere, and Lightroom users more ways to revise their work on Mac and iPhone.

At Adobe MAX on Tuesday, Adobe unveiled a bevy of features arriving now and over the coming months. As with many recent Adobe rollouts, most are AI-powered or AI-assisted.

Here's what it announced:

Photoshop

A new Relight tool adds light sources to an image, with controls for position, color, and brightness. The adjustments are nondestructive, allowing users to revise lighting without permanently changing the underlying image.

Generative Restyle creates variations from descriptions entered through Prompt to edit, then converts the result into a layer. A slider adjusts the effect's intensity without requiring another prompt.

The Remove Tool now detects related elements, including an object's footprints, reflections, shadows, and waves. It removes those elements alongside the object and reconstructs the surrounding area.

Image credit: Adobe

Quick Compare provides an on-canvas slider for reviewing before-and-after versions of an image. Users can compare changes without manually hiding individual layers.

AI Assisted Editor provides an interface centered on generative tools and natural-language prompts. Switching to the Pro Editor grants access to layers and full editing tools.

Photoshop's beta app adds Mockups for placing images or designs onto objects and surfaces. Camera Angles, also in beta, provides on-canvas controls for changing an entire image's viewpoint.

Generative Recompose, currently in beta, adapts images to different aspect ratios by repositioning the image and related elements. Convert to Text Layers, another beta feature, extracts text from flattened images and makes it editable.

Timelapse, also available in beta, records the editing process for sharing. Remove Ambient Effect Only, also in beta, removes effects such as haze, lens flare, shadows, and reflections while retaining objects.

Premiere

Color Mode is now generally available, providing a dedicated interface for video color grading. It supports basic corrections and more advanced grading adjustments.

The Generative Media tool adds video, sound effects, soundscape, and music generation directly within Premiere's timeline. It uses the edit's context to generate footage and audio users can refine.

Users can select Adobe Firefly models or partner models, including Google, Kling, Runway, and Luma. The tool generates supplemental footage, background music, and scene audio.

Enhance Audio separates dialogue, music, ambience, and sound effects so users can mix them independently. Separate Crosstalk isolates overlapping speakers into individual tracks.

Image credit: Adobe

Separate Sound Source breaks recordings into individual audio elements and supports cleaning up noisy dialogue. These controls provide separate access to sounds that were captured together.

Generative Remove, available in beta, removes unwanted objects directly from video clips in the timeline. Users mask and track an object, then apply Remove to fill the selected area while preserving the remaining footage.

Premiere mobile

Premiere on iPhone now offers hundreds of thousands of licensed tracks from Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group. Users can browse popular tracks and featured artists, including Olivia Dean and Noah Kahan.

Artist-inspired templates accompany songs, artists, and cultural moments within the app. The UMG and WMG music is licensed for personal, noncommercial videos, with Android availability coming soon.

Adobe Stock Audio remains available for projects requiring commercially licensed music. The new catalog's personal-use permissions do not cover those projects.

Adobe is also bringing AI Assistant to Premiere mobile through a private beta powered by its Creative Agent. The assistant generates editable first cuts and makes changes based on natural-language instructions.

Quick Cut lets users select camera-roll footage and describe the video they want to create. It generates a first cut that users can refine in the timeline.

AI Assistant also supports requests such as creating short videos from longer footage or assembling event highlights. Users can preview changes, adjust the results, or undo edits.

Lightroom

Glow adds lighting effects ranging from hazy diffusion to film-style halation. Users can apply presets or adjust how the light spreads through the image.

Blemish Removal expands beyond Lightroom's mobile app, adding controls for more detailed retouching. Users can apply an initial correction, then refine it while preserving skin features such as freckles.

Image credit: Adobe

Adobe is expanding and improving Camera Tethering across Lightroom on desktop and iPad. The changes support reviewing, organizing, and collaborating on images during a shoot.

Open Eyes, available in public beta, replaces closed eyes using a reference photo of the same person from the user's library. Users can select the reference themselves or let the feature find one.

Illustrator

Illustrator's updated content libraries add brushes, graphic styles, patterns, and gradients. New on-canvas Blend controls include a persistent control panel and live preview for adjusting designs.

InDesign

Co-editing, available in public beta, lets multiple designers work on the same layout simultaneously. Flex Layout dynamically resizes text frames as their content changes.

Check Document helps identify common editorial and accessibility issues during layout work. Rewrite adds text revision assistance within InDesign.

Creative Cloud AI integrations

Adobe is adding AI Assistant in beta to Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io. Users can describe multistep tasks, have the assistant execute them, and refine the results with each application's editing tools.

Image credit: Adobe

Adobe previewed Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations that connect third-party AI agents to Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects. They run locally on native project files, preserving editable layers, vectors, bins, and sequences.

These agents can apply a change across campaign assets or use connected services to retrieve briefs and share results. Adobe plans to bring the MCP integrations to Creative Cloud customers in early 2027.

Firefly

Firefly Video lets users arrange footage, plan a story, and add captions. It also generates transitions and supplemental footage for use in the edit.

Firefly Image provides tools to remove objects, change text, adjust lighting, and retouch photos. These edits target selected details while preserving the rest of the image.

Quick Actions provide preset workflows for creating thumbnails, building product advertisements, and applying trending styles to users' photos. These capabilities are available now alongside the Firefly Video and Image tools.

Firefly Design, available in beta, combines raster, vector, motion, 3D, and print work on one canvas. It includes editing tools, AI assistance, collaboration, client review, and export functions.

Firefly Graph, also in beta, combines AI models and Adobe product tools into reusable workflows. Users can adjust those workflows and share them with their teams.

Firefly Builder, being previewed in private beta, creates interactive app, website, and digital portfolio prototypes. It combines prompting with direct editing, allowing creators to explore multiple design directions.

Adobe's Creative Agent now supports brainstorming in Firefly Boards to develop mood boards, storyboards, and creative concepts. Users can also save preferred colors, styles, and brand guidelines for use across projects.

Firefly AI Assistant lets users review and adjust its plan before execution or allow it to proceed. Users can select image and video models themselves or let the assistant choose.

Adobe is previewing always-on agents in Firefly AI Assistant, with a beta scheduled for early 2027. These agents handle recurring background tasks, including organizing incoming footage, removing duplicate clips, and flagging camera shake or audio problems.

Image credit: Adobe

Users select a predefined agent, customize its workflow, set a goal, and review its plan before work begins. The agent calculates when tasks repeat, incorporates feedback, and requests decisions or approvals when needed.

A central Firefly dashboard lets users monitor progress, refine results, and approve work. Adobe will work with the creative community to develop the initial selection of predefined agents.

The news follows Monday's Adobe MAX announcement stating Adobe and The Walt Disney Company would enter a multi-year "strategic alliance." Adobe plans to explore concepts in Disney's innovation labs as well as parks and cruise development pipelines, using custom AI models and tools.

items.title: Criminals are using government-grade spyware to infect iPhones
items.content_html:
Sophisticated iPhone spyware once reserved for government surveillance is now being used by cybercriminals against ordinary users, with a new security report finding that criminal attacks account for most of its detections.

The findings come from mobile security firm iVerify's Advanced Mobile Threat Report 2026, published November 10. Researchers found 1.07 spyware infections per 1,000 consumer iOS scans, or roughly one in 900, while the rate dropped to 0.7 per 1,000 when enterprise devices were included.

The figures reflect iVerify's users, not the global iPhone population. Its consumer base has more than tripled since early 2025, although the report doesn't disclose total scans or infections.

The bigger shift is who's being targeted. Every enterprise infection linked to a criminal campaign involved a rank-and-file employee, not a high-profile executive.

Leaked iPhone exploits are giving criminals new opportunities

Much of the shift comes from two iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword, which security researchers publicly disclosed in March 2026.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group identified Coruna as a collection of 23 exploits organized into five attack chains targeting iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1. During 2025, researchers observed its use by a surveillance vendor's customer, followed by a suspected Russian espionage group targeting Ukrainian websites.

The same toolkit later appeared in widespread attacks operated by a financially motivated group in China. Google couldn't establish exactly how Coruna passed between those operators, but its research demonstrated how sophisticated exploitation techniques could spread beyond their original users.

DarkSword followed a similar trajectory. Researchers from Google, Lookout, and iVerify disclosed the exploit chain on March 18 after identifying its use by surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors.


The figures reflect iVerify's users, not the global iPhone population. Image credit: iVerify

The toolkit targeted iPhones running iOS 18.4 through iOS 18.7, exploiting six vulnerabilities to compromise devices and extract sensitive information. Apple addressed those vulnerabilities through subsequent security updates, with Google confirming that all six had been patched by iOS 26.3.

Both toolkits originally targeted specific older iOS releases, making software updates an important defense. The attacks documented in the report don't establish that the same exploit chains can compromise fully updated iPhones.

The subsequent release of DarkSword code gave criminals a starting point for developing their own variants without having to discover every vulnerability themselves.

iVerify has since identified modified versions capable of collecting additional passwords, messages, photographs, and cryptocurrency wallet information.

Malicious ads can infect vulnerable iPhones without a click

One of iVerify's more revealing cases involved an ordinary person who encountered two separate DarkSword attacks while browsing online. According to the company's telemetry, the first attack began when a malicious advertisement loaded during an Instagram browsing session.

The person didn't click the advertisement, but the exploit still started running on the vulnerable device.

A second attack occurred later after the same person followed a link. Researchers identified a different DarkSword variant associated with another threat actor, although both attacks appeared intended to steal cryptocurrency.

The technique is known as a half-click attack because malicious code can begin executing when an advertisement loads, without requiring the victim to interact with it.

Advertising networks let criminals narrow their targets using details such as device type, iOS version, location, and interests. Attackers can use that information to deliver exploits specifically to iPhones running vulnerable software.

The approach combines the reach of online advertising with the ability to target specific vulnerabilities. Someone browsing a legitimate website or scrolling through social media could encounter an attack without downloading anything or visiting a suspicious page.


The approach combines the reach of online advertising with the ability to target specific vulnerabilities. Image credit: iVerify

Criminals have also hijacked legitimate websites through abandoned tracking scripts. In October, researchers uncovered a campaign that used an expired analytics domain to redirect visitors from thousands of online stores to malicious servers distributing DarkSword and Coruna.

The victims didn't need to visit a fraudulent storefront because the compromised code was already embedded in otherwise legitimate websites.

App Store protections aren't completely immune

The report also highlights FomoPeek, a cryptocurrency monitoring app that carried a hidden exploitation toolkit in versions distributed through Apple's App Store in September. Security researchers at SlowMist and OKX found malicious components in versions 1.1 and 1.2.

The toolkit could exploit iOS vulnerabilities, escape the app sandbox, and access data belonging to other apps.

The affected versions appeared on September 9 and September 12, before an update removed the malicious components on September 17. SlowMist's investigation traced approximately $580,000 in stolen USDT to a cryptocurrency address associated with the operation.

Researchers confirmed the toolkit's ability to collect application data in a controlled environment, including information from Apple Notes. Their findings don't establish that every supported exploit succeeded or that every targeted cryptocurrency wallet was compromised.

FomoPeek is one documented case rather than evidence of widespread App Store exploitation. Still, it demonstrates that Apple's review process cannot guarantee every approved app is free from malicious code.

Apple threat notifications don't cover every attack

Detecting a successful compromise presents another problem because newer spyware variants can erase evidence before security researchers have an opportunity to investigate. DarkSword can collect stored credentials and other information without maintaining a persistent infection.

Newer variants also remove additional logs and working files, making it harder to reconstruct an attack after the malware has finished running.

A compromised work iPhone could expose credentials for corporate email, messaging platforms, and other services. Criminals could then use those credentials to access accounts beyond the infected device.


The toolkit could exploit iOS vulnerabilities, escape the app sandbox, and access data belonging to other apps. Image credit: iVerify

iVerify reports that none of the devices it confirmed as infected with DarkSword or Coruna received an Apple threat notification.

Apple's warning system has a narrower purpose, however. The company says its notifications are designed for people believed to have been individually targeted by mercenary spyware, typically because of their identity or activities.

The absence of a warning therefore doesn't establish that Apple's system failed at its intended purpose, nor should users interpret silence as proof that their device hasn't been compromised.

The report warns that AI is accelerating exploit development, although iVerify's testing found limits to its effectiveness. Researchers examined suspected AI-assisted attempts to adapt DarkSword for newer iOS versions, but none successfully exploited the devices tested.

Keeping iOS updated remains one of the best defenses against these attacks, since security patches close vulnerabilities that criminals continue to exploit. Installing apps from trusted sources also reduces exposure to other forms of malware.

iVerify recommends extending mobile security monitoring beyond executives, particularly when employees use personal phones for work. The company sells mobile detection products, giving it a commercial interest in recommending continuous monitoring.

The findings don't mean every iPhone can be silently compromised. They show how criminals can reuse sophisticated exploits against vulnerable devices, putting ordinary users at risk alongside traditional surveillance targets.

How to protect your iPhone from spyware

Keeping your iPhone updated is the most effective defense against the exploit chains documented by iVerify. Open Settings, select General, then Software Update to check for available patches.

You can also enable automatic installation under Automatic Updates so your iPhone receives future fixes without requiring you to check manually.

Only download apps from trusted sources, and check the developer before installing unfamiliar software. Apple's App Store provides security protections, but the FomoPeek incident shows that approved apps aren't automatically safe.

Using strong, unique passwords and two-factor authentication also helps protect accounts, although neither can guarantee protection if the device itself is compromised.

People concerned about sophisticated, targeted spyware can consider Lockdown Mode, which restricts certain apps, websites, and features to reduce potential attack paths. Apple designed the feature for people facing unusually serious surveillance threats, so most iPhone owners won't need it.

items.title: The OLED iPad Air is still expected to launch in early 2027
items.content_html:
The iPad Air refresh for early 2027 will include the OLED display technology update in both of its sizes, a report claims.

The OLED upgrade for the iPad Air has been rumored for a while, and has previously been tipped to be launched sometime in early 2027. In a report on Tuesday, it seems that OLED will be included across both display sizes for the tablet model.

According to sources of DigiTimes, Apple is still targeting a launch of the OLED iPad Air in the first half of 2027. Both the 11-inch and 13-inch models are anticipated to get the display technology.

It is expected to be a similar display to the iPad mini, using a single-stack design with a low-temperature polycrystalline silicon (LTPS) backplane. The iPad Pro will continue to have a much brighter display, thanks to having a pair of OLED layers instead of one, and the use of a low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) backplane instead.

The tech choice also means there won't be ProMotion support in the iPad Air, if the report is true.

Samsung Display is believed to be the main supplier of the display panels for the iPad Air. BOE is reportedly still trying to become a supplier, but has yet to meet Apple's requirements.

As for shipments, it is thought that there will be between 4 million and 5 million units of the iPad Air shipping in 2027, across both sizes of screen. The iPad mini should do similar numbers, with iPad Pro possibly seeing a dip down to 4 million.

items.title: Three workers die at Tata's iPhone factory in India
items.content_html:
Apple and Tata are assisting local authorities over the deaths of three maintenance workers at the iPhone plant in Tamil Nadu.

The Tata iPhone factory is one that has previously been threatened with being shut down over environmental concerns. Now according to Reuters, three contract workers have died while inspecting an effluent treatment plant on the site.

The deaths happened late on November 9, 2026. The three workers reportedly inhaled an unspecified gas while they were inspecting an external nano-filtration tank operated on the site by Nalco Water.

"We take this incident extremely seriously," said a spokesperson from Nalco Water. The company is part of Ecolab, headquartered in the US, and the spokesperson said that the workers were engaged by one of its subcontractors.

State officials say that alongside their own investigation, both Tata and Apple will be examining the scene. A team from Apple is reportedly now visiting the plant in order to assist the local authorities.

Production of iPhones was not affected, as the plant was closed for the Diwali festival.

Neither Tata nor Apple has commented publicly. Tamil Nadu's industries minister posted on X/Twitter that the incident will be "thoroughly investigated and appropriate action will be taken based on the findings."

Tata's iPhone plant

The plant in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, is one that Indian health authorities accused of contaminating local water supplies. Regulators later dropped this accusation, however.

This is the plant that the Tata Group bought from iPhone assembly firm Wistron back in 2023. Prior to it being bought, Apple had put Wistron on probation in 2020 because of poor living conditions that had prompted worker riots.

Apple in India

The Tata Group is a major supplier of iPhones to Apple, exceeded only by Foxconn. Reportedly Tata is responsible for around 40% of India's iPhone production.

Apple has been steadily increasing its reliance on India for many years in a move to lessen its dependence on China. That is partly because of trade tensions between the US and China, but also because of the risks of relying on a single source.

India has been planning tax breaks to encourage Apple to expand in the country. By January 2026, India was said to have exported $50 billion worth of iPhones over the preceding five years.

items.title: Meta's Muse AI now has an Apple Watch app, which you shouldn't install
items.content_html:
Meta's AI agent has made its way to the Apple Watch, but all potential benefits are outweighed by the inherent risk associated with the tool, not to mention the privacy implications.

Following its expansion to the iPad in October 2026, Meta's Muse has received an Apple Watch companion app. The change was disclosed via the App Store page for Muse, which details the changes in version 15.0 of the iOS app.

"Add Muse to your wrist with the new Apple Watch Companion app," reads the description. On the Apple Watch, users can now call and talk to Meta's virtual assistant, text it, or use dictation with Muse.

The assistant can also perform tasks like booking event tickets, among other things. Meta emphasizes that Muse can be linked with other Meta apps, including Facebook and Instagram, as well as with users' calendar, email, and finance apps.

Meta says Muse can audit subscriptions, track expenses, flag forgotten charges, and more. However, trusting Meta's virtual assistant with your financial information isn't exactly the best idea, to say the least.

Despite Meta's claims that users can "approve actions before they happen," Muse has been found to have a mind of its own. In September 2026, Muse synced 187,000 lines from a user's Apple Messages database on macOS, despite Full Disk Access being off.

Meta's AI companion did so without permission. One can only imagine the data it might harvest if given access to someone's financial information or the data stored on an Apple Watch.

In all fairness, at the very bottom of the App Store page for Muse, Meta acknowledges that its AI agent "may be inaccurate or take unexpected actions." Users are also instructed to "check in" and "intervene as needed."

Of course, that hasn't stopped Meta from pushing Muse across platforms and applications, with projects such as Muse Code meant to take on Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's ChatGPT Codex.

Given Meta's history, however, Muse is an app best avoided across all platforms and devices. Siri AI is already available on the Apple Watch, Mac, iPad, iPhone, and more, and Apple's long-standing privacy commitments are still in place.

items.title: Unauthorized Bluetooth pairing & iMessage snooping patched in iOS 27.2.1
items.content_html:
Apple's iOS 27.2.1 update brings key security fixes that stop attackers from accessing your iMessage group chats and pairing with your iPhone via Bluetooth.

On Monday, two weeks after the arrival of iOS 27.2, Apple deployed the iOS 27.2.1 update. Though the release doesn't include any new features, it fixes several security issues related to iMessage and Bluetooth.

Notably, iOS 27.2.1 addresses CoreUtils issues that allowed malicious Bluetooth devices to pair with iPhones and bypass the pairing code limit without user interaction. Apple fixed these two vulnerabilities with improved checks and enhancements to state management.

Similarly, Apple resolved a vulnerability that let attackers bypass the AirPlay pairing code limit. Also related to Bluetooth is a now-patched use-after-free vulnerability that let bad actors corrupt process memory. Apple used improved memory management to resolve the issue.

In addition to Bluetooth security patches, iOS 27.2.1 also brings two fixes for iMessage. Monday's update prevents attackers from joining iMessage group chats.

It also stops attackers from reading group chat messages sent before they joined. Apple removed vulnerable code and fixed an authorization issue to address these problems.

Also found in the iOS 27.2.1 update is a fix for an App Intents authorization issue, which gave apps access to sensitive user data. Improved state management was used to patch the vulnerability.

Though iMessage and Bluetooth fixes are by far the most significant in iOS 27.2.1, Apple also patched a Brotli out-of-bounds write issue that enabled memory corruption. This was resolved through improved input validation.

All of the security fixes in iOS 27.2.1 can be found on Apple's website. Though relatively light patch-wise, compared to the more than 130 fixes included with iOS 27.2, Monday's software release should be installed by all users.

items.title: Apple Creator Studio users can pay for higher Apple Intelligence usage limits
items.content_html:
Users of Apple Creator Studio who run into Apple Intelligence limits will be able to pay for extra usage, via a new usage pack.

With a few exceptions, Apple has avoided forcing users to pay for extra access to features powered by Apple Intelligence. On Monday, it's started to roll out a new charge aimed at Apple Creator Studio users.

Anyone who uses Apple Intelligence features in Apple's suite of tools will find that there are usage limits as part of the monthly subscription.

This includes features like image generation, shape generation, and super resolution in Keynote, Pages, Numbers, and Freeform, as well as parts of Pixelmator Pro and the new Assistant in Logic Pro for Mac.

The Logic Pro update from October 27 with the Assistant has a "Show Usage" bar under the Menu Bar option "Intelligence Features." The Usage window, labeled as in beta, includes a button offering to "Buy More Usage."

If you click the button, you will be given the option to pay for a $49.99 "Intelligence usage pack." So far, it appears that the option only appears in Logic Pro, but it will almost certainly spread to other apps in the collection.

Extra use, but with limits

The small print for these Intelligence Usage Packs, spotted by 9to5Mac, explains that the extra packs provide an additional allowance on top of what is provided in the Apple Creator Studio subscription.

Normally, that initial allowance can generate up to 50 images, 250 shapes, 50 presentations of 8 to 10 slides each, or presenter notes for 700 slides. That allowance resets each month.

Under the terms, the Intelligence Usage Packs are a one-time purchase, available in the U.S. Canada, UK, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, India, and Mexico.

The packs also do not support Family Sharing, and can only be used by the account that the user was using for iCloud at the time of purchase.

If a pack is not completely consumed, it can roll over into the next month, and continue to be used once that month's allowance has been exhausted. The pack itself will expire 12 months after purchase if left untouched.

items.title: If you're getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone
items.content_html:
The new MacBook Pro uses pulse width modulation that is inducing eye strain, and headaches for some new buyers. Here's what pulse width modulation is, why it may cause problems for some users, and what you can do about it.

In short, the PROLED MacBook Pro is constantly strobing the user at a bad combination of frequency and amplitude. It's not as obvious as a flashing light at a rave or party, or light filtered through helicopter blades, but it is happening constantly, at close range.

Some people are susceptible to potentially serious health issues from those strobing lights. Others may have existing health conditions that are aggravated by the flashing lights.

Video game publishers have warned about this kind of thing for some time, and the concept has been used by trolls to attack people with epilepsy. The health issues aren't as bad as what the Apple Vision Pro can induce given the wide field of vision that headset fills, but given that this is the first time that the technology has come to the MacBook Pro, it's worth talking about again.

Here's why that all matters, and who it matters to.

Health issues from strobing lights, and who is affected

We are not medical doctors here at AppleInsider, but this author had a child that was profoundly epileptic, and we did talk to neurologists before writing this article for Apple Vision Pro first, and now again for this version of the article for MacBook Pro.

We're comfortable writing this article given this mix of practical experience and professional consultation.

There are three main types of health impacts from strobing lights — flicker vertigo, photosensitive epilepsy, and general photosensitivity.

Flicker Vertigo happens at refresh rates between 1Hz and 20Hz, and can cause disorientation, nausea, and rapid eye movement.

It was first spotted in early helicopters, watching the sun strobe through a rotating helicopter blade. It is less common on the road, but still can be seen by the driver and passengers as the sun filters through trees as a car drives through a lightly wooded area.

Flicker Vertigo is common, but fortunately the symptoms vanish when the strobing stops. It is not incredibly relevant to MacBook Pro owners, unless they are hit with maliciously crafted content — which as we've mentioned happens from time to time.

Photosensitive epilepsy is far less common, but far more dangerous. While sensitivities vary, any strobing can induce a seizure in folks with photosensitive epilepsy. The individual circumstances and severity of the seizure can vary, person to person.

And, it is possible for somebody to not have any other outward signs of epilepsy, and still be susceptible to specific photosensitive triggers that they previously weren't aware of.

Other health conditions can be aggravated by strobing light. A very high percentage of traumatic brain injury sufferers report photosensitivity, as do people with migraines, frequent tension headaches, or cluster headaches.

If you've ever been told you have photophobia, the Apple Vision Pro and the new PROLED MacBook Pro are probably not for you.

Sensitivity to strobing lights is also aggravated by fatigue of any sort, diet, time of exposure to the strobing and a host of other situations. If you're well-rested, you may not be sensitive to strobing lights.

If you've skipped a meal, are pulling an all-nighter in front of your MacBook Pro, and didn't get any sleep the previous night, that's about the worst-case scenario.

In all of these cases, the situation is aggravated as more of the user's field of vision is impacted by the strobing. In the case of the Apple Vision Pro, the user's entire field of vision is covered by the strobing from the Pulse Width Modulation used to control the screens' brightness and color mix.

For the new MacBook Pro, it's not the entire field of vision, but it is a wide one. The pulse width modulation, which is not the same as the screen refresh rate, is running at 240Hz on the new MacBook Pro, with a 56% flicker amplitude. This is the same as it is on modern iPhones, but it is also on a much larger screen.

For instance, Pulse width modulation exists in non-OLED screens too. The M4 Pro Mini-LED MacBook has a 14,880 Hz pulse width modulation, which is better for nearly everybody.

Clearly, not everybody is impacted by strobing lights, and even so, frequency sensitivity can vary. This is good, considering the LED light bulbs that have replaced incandescent lights flicker, although less than the fluorescent bulbs that were a stop-gap between the Edison incandescent bulb and the newer LED.

That's cold comfort to the people who are hit, though. And, it's why Genius Bars we've spoken to are getting complaints, and retailers are seeing returns of the hardware at a bit higher rate than normal.

Just because you're not having an issue, doesn't mean that it's not a problem.

What is Pulse Width Modulation?

There is a lot to Pulse Width Modulation in electronics as a whole, but as it pertains to Apple hardware, Pulse Width Modulation is what Apple uses by default to regulate the brightness of individual color cells in the eye displays.

An incandescent bulb that can dim throws off fewer photons when at a lower wattage, roughly proportional to the magnitude of the cut in power. Provide half the power to an incandescent bulb, and it will be about half as bright.

It does not turn off quickly and strobe. Incandescents just emits fewer photons because of the lower power.

In an OLED display such as that used in the MacBook Pro, brightness control and color mixing is accomplished by turning individual color cells on and off very quickly. If full power, constantly, is being applied to a color cell, then that cell is "on time" or at a 100% duty cycle, and is fully bright.

Pulse width modulation and duty cycle example - credit circuitdigest.com

While there is an overall screen refresh frequency factor to consider as it pertains to health, in short, given a fixed frequency, to reduce the brightness, at default settings, the color cell is extremely rapidly turned on and off. A 50% duty cycle has the cell on or off half of the time, and is about half the brightness. It also effectively strobes the user at a different frequency than the display as a whole is doing.

Pulse Width Modulation has been used in OLED iPhones since the iPhone X, and it is vital to the operation of the screen. It has always been a concern at some level, to some people. However, the iPhone is a hand-held device, not occupying the a large percentage of field of vision that the Apple Vision Pro and PROLED MacBook Pro maintain.

How bad is this?

We've been watching for reports of photosensitivity since the new iPad mini and PROLED MacBook Pro launched, like we did for Apple Vision Pro. There are periodic social media reports of headaches and fatigue.

The advice is clear from the doctors we've spoken to, and from Apple itself. If you start feeling strange in any way while using Apple Vision Pro, and now MacBook Pro, stop using it, and schedule an appoint with your doctor.

And, watch for symptoms in folks that you care about that are new owners. It's easy to get over-excited about new technology, and use it for far more than you should in the early days.

Apple has help for this on the iPhone, but not yet the MacBook Pro.

No good way to reduce strobing from the MacBook Pro

There's a setting on iPad mini, and iPhones after the iPhone 17, called Display Pulse Smoothing. It lives in Accessibility, and when the feature is on, it disables pulse width modulation and uses voltage dimming to provide a different way to dim the OLED display.

This is not in macOS. At least, not yet.

As of November 10, 2026, if you know you're sensitive to Pulse Width Modulation or strobing, do not buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED display. Stick with the previous models.

items.title: Incremental iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS, macOS updates arrive with bug fixes
items.content_html:
Apple has issued updates for iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS 27.2.1, and macOS 27.2.1, with the incremental update bringing a collection of bug fixes and performance improvements to users.

Apple released its 27.2 operating system updates on October 26 and is currently running a developer beta for the 27.3 updates. That hasn't stopped it from issuing a small update for the current version.

The updates are small, as the point release number .1 indicates, so you typically shouldn't expect feature updates at all. They are more updates that have bug fixes, security updates, and performance improvements, which you really should update your device to as soon as possible.

Slightly differing from previous incremental updates, users may see different build numbers for their products as opposed to the mainline release. Apple has created versions specific to some products, such as the iPhone Duo and the PROLED MacBook Pro.

Apple has since detailed the security content of the patches.

The full list of updates are:

  • iOS 27.2.1 (Build number 24B8156)
  • iOS 27.2.1 (24B91034) for iPhone Duo
  • iPadOS 27.2.1 (24B8156)
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B131)
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B7131) for M6 MacBook Pro and iMac
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B8132) for PROLED MacBook Pro
  • visionOS 27.2.1 (24N124)
  • watchOS 27.2.1 (24S132)

Apple also issued updates for earlier operating system generations:

  • iOS 26.7.3 (23H131)
  • iOS 18.7.12 (22H390)
  • iPadOS 26.7.3 (23H131)
  • iPadOS 18.7.12 (22H390)
  • macOS 26.7.3 (25G342)
  • macOS 15.8.3 (24H241)
  • watchOS 26.6.1 (23U95)

How to install iOS 27.2.1 on an iPhone

To manually install iOS 27.2.1 on an iPhone, open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update. Tap the iOS 27.2.1 update and follow the instructions.

If you have automatic updates enabled, this will be performed on your behalf.
